title: A.1 Kinematics
subject: IBDP Physics
introduction: Kinematics is the branch of physics that studies the motion of objects without analysing the forces responsible for that motion. It describes how objects move using measurable quantities such as position, distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration. Kinematics provides the foundation for mechanics and is used in many areas of physics, engineering and technology.
learning_objectives: Understand the difference between scalar and vector quantities.
Explain the difference between speed and velocity.
Calculate acceleration using changes in velocity.
Apply equations of motion for objects with constant acceleration.

definitions.meaning: The location of an object relative to a chosen reference point.
The total path travelled by an object. Distance is a scalar quantity.
The change in position from the starting point to the final point in a specific direction. Displacement is a vector quantity.
The rate at which distance changes with time.
The rate at which displacement changes with time. Velocity includes direction.
The rate of change of velocity with time.

core_concepts.heading: Distance and Displacement
core_concepts.explanation: Distance measures the complete path travelled by an object. It does not include direction. Displacement measures the shortest straight-line change from the initial position to the final position and includes direction.

core_concepts.heading: Scalar and Vector Quantities
core_concepts.explanation: Scalar quantities have magnitude only, while vector quantities have both magnitude and direction. Distance and speed are scalars. Displacement and velocity are vectors.

core_concepts.heading: Speed and Velocity
core_concepts.explanation: Speed tells how fast an object moves. Velocity tells how fast an object moves in a particular direction. An object moving in a circle at constant speed still has changing velocity because its direction changes.

core_concepts.heading: Acceleration
core_concepts.explanation: Acceleration occurs when velocity changes. An object accelerates when it speeds up, slows down or changes direction.

formulas.name: Average velocity
formulas.explanation: Average velocity describes the displacement of an object divided by the time taken. It includes direction because displacement is a vector quantity.

formulas.name: Acceleration
formulas.explanation: Acceleration measures how quickly velocity changes. A positive value shows increasing velocity, while a negative value shows decreasing velocity.

formulas.name: First equation of motion
formulas.explanation: This equation is used when acceleration remains constant.

formulas.name: Second equation of motion
formulas.explanation: This equation calculates displacement when initial velocity, acceleration and time are known.

formulas.name: Third equation of motion
formulas.explanation: This equation is useful when time is not provided.

motion_graphs.explanation: A distance-time graph shows how distance changes with time. The gradient of the graph represents speed.
important_points: A straight line shows constant speed.
A steeper line represents higher speed.
A horizontal line represents an object at rest.

motion_graphs.explanation: A velocity-time graph shows how velocity changes with time. The gradient represents acceleration.
important_points: Area under the graph gives displacement.

motion_graphs.explanation: An acceleration-time graph shows how acceleration changes with time.
important_points: The area under the graph represents change in velocity.
A horizontal line shows constant acceleration.

worked_examples.question: A car increases its velocity from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 10 seconds. Calculate acceleration.
A car starts from rest and accelerates at 4 m/s² for 5 seconds. Find final velocity.

common_mistakes: Confusing distance with displacement. Distance has no direction, while displacement includes direction.
Using speed and velocity as the same quantity. Velocity requires direction.
Forgetting to convert units before calculation.
Using the wrong equation of motion when acceleration is not constant.
Reading the gradient of a graph incorrectly.
Forgetting that the area under a velocity-time graph represents displacement.
Ignoring negative signs when dealing with direction.
ib_exam_tips: Write the correct equation before substituting values.
Always include SI units in the final answer.
Show every step of calculation clearly.
Use significant figures according to the data provided.
Label graphs with correct axes and units.
Explain answers using physics terms instead of only calculations.

hl_extension.explanation: Projectile motion describes objects moving under the influence of gravity after being launched. Horizontal and vertical motion are analysed separately because gravity only affects vertical motion.
Relative motion describes the velocity of an object compared to another moving reference frame.
Higher level physics uses calculus concepts to analyse changing velocity and acceleration.

real_world_applications: Vehicle safety systems use kinematics to calculate stopping distances.
Aircraft engineers use motion analysis to study takeoff and landing.
Sports scientists analyse athlete movement using velocity and acceleration data.
Space missions use kinematics to calculate spacecraft trajectories.

practice_questions.question: A runner travels 100 m in 20 seconds. Calculate average speed.
A car accelerates from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 seconds. Calculate acceleration.
A projectile is launched horizontally. Explain why horizontal velocity remains constant while vertical velocity changes.
practice_questions.answer: Gravity only acts vertically, so horizontal motion has constant velocity while vertical motion accelerates due to gravity.

summary: Kinematics provides the mathematical tools needed to describe motion. By understanding displacement, velocity, acceleration and motion graphs, students are able to analyse and predict the movement of objects. These concepts form the foundation for mechanics and are essential for further topics in IB Physics.
